_note: The Gym manifest (WP25a): which grammar points act as selectable form categories, grouped into picker columns. 'point' must match the grammar point title exactly (resolved to ids at request time). 'usage' is the plain-language hover explanation; 'example' is a real drill sentence from that point. 'nonstandard': entries hidden behind the 'include non-standard words' toggle.

entries.label: Present (polite)
entries.usage: What happens now or regularly — the everyday 요-form.
entries.example: 저는 학교에 가요. — I go to school.

entries.label: Past
entries.usage: What already happened: 았/었 slides in before the ending.
entries.example: 어제 학교에 갔어요. — I went to school yesterday.

entries.label: Future
entries.usage: Plans and predictions with (으)ㄹ 거예요.
entries.example: 내일 학교에 갈 거예요. — I will go to school tomorrow.

entries.label: Formal ㅂ니다
entries.usage: The news-and-business register: 갑니다, 먹습니다.
entries.example: 저는 매일 회사에 갑니다. — I go to the office every day.

entries.point: Ongoing and resulting: 고 있어요 / 아·어 있어요 (자고 있어요)
entries.label: Progressive
entries.usage: In the middle of doing: 고 있어요.
entries.example: 지금 밥을 먹고 있어요. — I'm eating right now.

entries.label: Can / can't
entries.usage: Ability and impossibility with (으)ㄹ 수 있어요/없어요.
entries.example: 저는 한국어를 할 수 있어요. — I can speak Korean.

entries.point: Must and may: 아/어야 해요, 아/어도 돼요 (가야 해요)
entries.label: Must / may
entries.usage: Obligation (야 해요) and permission (도 돼요).
entries.example: 지금 집에 가야 해요. — I have to go home now.

entries.point: Irregular verbs: ㅂ, ㄷ, 르 (추워요, 들어요, 몰라요)
entries.label: Irregular stems
entries.usage: The ㅂ/ㄷ/르 families transform before vowel endings: 춥다 → 추워요.
entries.example: 오늘 날씨가 정말 추워요. — The weather is really cold today.

entries.point: Honorific machinery: 께서, 드리다, 뵙다 (선생님께서 말씀하셨어요)
entries.label: Honorific forms
entries.usage: Raising the subject with 께서 + 시, humbling yourself with 드리다/뵙다.
entries.example: 선생님께서 오셨어요. — The teacher has arrived.

entries.label: Copula 이다
entries.usage: Attach 이다 / 야·이야 / 예요·이에요 to a noun to say 'X is Y'.

entries.point: Present Tense Conjugation of 이다 / 아니다
entries.label: 이다 – present
entries.usage: Attach 이다 to a noun to say 'is/am/are' at the right politeness level.

entries.point: Past Tense Conjugation of 이다 / 아니다
entries.label: 이다 – past
entries.usage: Attach ~이었/~였 plus a politeness ending to a noun to say 'was/were'.

entries.label: ~ㄹ/을 것이다 (future)
entries.usage: Add ~ㄹ/을 to the stem, then 것/거 + 이다 to say 'will …'.

entries.label: Irregulars + ~ㄹ/을
entries.usage: Apply ㅅ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㄹ irregular changes when adding ~ㄹ/을 to a stem.

entries.point: Passive verbs with ~아/어 있다 (describing a state)
entries.label: Passive state ~아/어 있다
entries.usage: Turn a passive verb into a 'is currently in this state' form.

entries.point: Passive/active pairs with 나다 and 내다
entries.label: 나다 / 내다 pairs
entries.usage: Pick the passive (나다) or active (내다) member of the pair.

entries.point: 나다 with nouns (기억이 나다, 화가 나다, 땀이 나다…)
entries.label: Noun + 나다
entries.usage: Say that a feeling, memory or event 'comes up' (subject takes ~이/가).

entries.label: Compound verbs (~아/어 + verb)
entries.usage: Join two verbs with ~아/어 to form one compound verb.

entries.label: Sequential ~아/어서
entries.usage: Verb stem + ~아/어서 when the first action leads directly into the second (가다/오다, 앉다/서다/눕다).

entries.label: Want to (~고 싶다)
entries.usage: Verb stem + ~고 싶다, conjugated like an adjective, to say 'want to do'.

entries.label: ~고 있다 (progressive)
entries.usage: Verb stem + ~고 있다 for an action going on right now

entries.label: ~아/어 있다 (resulting state)
entries.usage: Verb stem + ~아/어 있다 for the state left after the action

entries.label: ~아/어지다 tenses
entries.usage: Conjugate 'become + adjective' like any verb

entries.label: ~ㅂ/습니까? (formal question)
entries.usage: Formal high-respect question ending: ~ㅂ니까 after a vowel, ~습니까 after a consonant

entries.label: ~니 questions
entries.usage: Informal question ending, usable in all tenses

entries.label: ~나(요) soft questions
entries.usage: Softly ask a question with a verb or 있다/없다

entries.label: ~기 전에
entries.usage: Verb stem + ~기 전에 = 'before doing something'; no tense inside the clause.

entries.label: ~ㄴ/은 후에
entries.usage: Verb stem + ~은 (consonant) / ~ㄴ (vowel) + 후에 = 'after doing'.

entries.label: Topic 은/는
entries.usage: What the sentence is about: 는 after vowels, 은 after consonants.
entries.example: 저는 학생이에요. — I am a student.

entries.label: Subject 이/가
entries.usage: Who or what does it — new information takes 이/가.
entries.example: 친구가 와요. — A friend is coming.

entries.point: Object particle 을/를 and verb-last order (밥을 먹어요)
entries.label: Object 을/를
entries.usage: The thing acted on: 를 after vowels, 을 after consonants.

entries.point: Place and time: 에 vs 에서 (집에, 집에서)
entries.label: 에 vs 에서
entries.usage: Destination/time/being-there = 에; where an action happens = 에서.
entries.example: 도서관에서 공부해요. — I study at the library.

entries.label: 하고 / 도
entries.usage: 하고 joins nouns or means 'with'; 도 replaces the particle to say 'too'.
entries.example: 빵하고 우유를 샀어요. — I bought bread and milk.

entries.label: Comparison 보다
entries.usage: X보다 = more than X; 제일/가장 = the most.
entries.example: 형은 저보다 커요. — My brother is taller than me.

entries.label: Reason 아/어서
entries.usage: Reasons and lead-in sequences; no commands after it.
entries.example: 배가 고파서 밥을 먹었어요. — I was hungry, so I ate.

entries.label: Reason (으)니까
entries.usage: The reason connector that CAN introduce commands and suggestions.
entries.example: 시간이 없으니까 빨리 가세요. — There's no time, so go quickly.

entries.label: If (으)면
entries.usage: Conditions and habitual whens.
entries.example: 비가 오면 집에 있을 거예요. — If it rains, I'll stay home.

entries.point: But and and: 지만, 고 (춥지만, 먹고)
entries.label: But / and
entries.usage: 지만 contrasts; 고 lists and sequences.
entries.example: 날씨가 춥지만 갈 거예요. — It's cold, but I'll go.

entries.label: Noun modifiers
entries.usage: Whole clauses describe nouns from the front — Korean's relative clauses.
entries.example: 지금 읽는 책이 재미있어요. — The book I'm reading is interesting.

entries.label: Quotes 다고
entries.usage: Fold what someone said into your sentence.
entries.example: 친구가 내일 온다고 해요. — My friend says he's coming tomorrow.

entries.label: Topic ~는/은
entries.usage: Attach the subject particle, choosing the form by the noun's final sound.

entries.label: Object ~를/을
entries.usage: Attach the object particle to the noun the verb acts on.

entries.label: 이것/그것/저것
entries.usage: Use the demonstrative pronouns as subject or object.

entries.label: Number + counter
entries.usage: Put a pure Korean number and a counter after the noun being counted.

entries.point: Counters with numbers (개, 명, 대, 잔)
entries.label: Counters
entries.usage: Number + counter for counting nouns (개, 명, 대, 잔)

entries.label: Months of the year
entries.usage: Sino-Korean number + 월 to name a calendar month

entries.label: Topic vs subject particle
entries.usage: ~는/은 for general facts and comparisons; ~이/가 for a specific, just-noticed situation.

entries.label: 모두 (all / everybody)
entries.usage: Adverbially = 다; as a pronoun it takes particles (모두가, 모두를, 모두에게).

entries.label: 아무나 / 아무도
entries.usage: 아무나 = anybody (positive sentence); 아무도 = nobody (negative predicate required).

entries.label: 아무 + 거/데/때
entries.usage: ~나 for 'anything/anywhere/anytime'; ~도 for 'nothing/nowhere' with a negative verb.

entries.label: Noun + ~마다
entries.usage: Attach ~마다 to a noun to mean 'each/every' one of it.

entries.point: 있다 with ~이/가: to have, to be at a location
entries.label: 있다 + ~이/가
entries.usage: Mark the possessed thing with ~이/가 before 있다.

entries.point: Turning adjectives into verbs with ~아/어하다 (좋아하다, 싫어하다)
entries.label: ~아/어하다 verbs
entries.usage: Make a feeling-adjective into a verb that can take an object.

entries.point: Comparing with 다르다/비슷하다/같다 and the particle ~와/과/랑/이랑/하고
entries.label: Comparison adjectives (polite)
entries.usage: Say X is different from / similar to / the same as Y using ~와/과

entries.label: Adjective → noun modifier (~ㄴ/은)
entries.usage: Describe a noun with an adjective or a whole comparison phrase

entries.point: Talking about pain and sickness: 아프다 and ~에 걸리다
entries.label: 아프다 (ㅡ irregular)
entries.usage: Say a body part hurts (with 이/가) or that someone was sick

entries.label: ~적 / ~적으로 / ~적이다
entries.usage: Turn a Chinese-origin noun into a descriptive word, an adverb, or an adjective

entries.label: ~스럽다 (ㅂ irregular)
entries.usage: Say something has the properties of a noun: lovely, natural, disappointing

entries.label: ~스럽다 adjectives
entries.usage: Noun + ~스럽다 makes an adjective; ㅂ-irregular, modifier ~스러운, adverb ~스럽게.

entries.label: ~아/어지다 (become + adj)
entries.usage: Adjective stem + ~아/어지다 turns 'be ___' into 'get/become ___'

entries.label: 낫다 (ㅅ-irregular)
entries.usage: Say 'better' in an explicit comparison; ㅅ drops before vowels

entries.label: ~ㄴ/은가(요) soft questions
entries.usage: Softly ask about a present state with an adjective or 이다

entries.label: 어때 (opinion) forms
entries.usage: Ask someone's evaluation of something, present or past

entries.label: 이/그/저
entries.usage: Pick the right 'this/that' word before a noun.

entries.label: Sino-Korean numbers
entries.usage: Combine 일~십, 백, 천, 만 to build numbers for money, time and math.

entries.label: Saying zero: 영 vs 공
entries.usage: Pick 영 for math, scores and temperatures; 공 when reciting digits like phone or room numbers.

entries.label: Clock time (시/분)
entries.usage: Pure Korean number + 시 for the hour, Sino-Korean number + 분 for the minutes

entries.label: Ordinals (번째)
entries.usage: Number + 번째 = first/second/third…, with 첫 for 'first'

entries.point: Shortened ordinals: 첫째, 둘째, 셋째, 넷째
entries.label: Short ordinals (첫째)
entries.usage: 첫째/둘째/셋째/넷째 for one's children and for listing points

entries.label: Months (달/개월)
entries.usage: 두 달 (pure Korean) or 이 개월 (Sino-Korean) for an amount of months
entries.example: 저는 두 달 동안 한국어를 공부했어요.

entries.point: Pure Korean vs Sino-Korean numbers with time counters
entries.label: Number system by counter
entries.usage: Chinese-origin time words take Sino-Korean numbers; native ones take pure Korean numbers
entries.example: 저는 두 달 동안, 즉 이 개월 동안 공부했어요.

entries.point: ~는/은 vs ~이/가: general statements and immediate experience
entries.label: Topic 는/은 vs subject 이/가
entries.usage: Use 는/은 for general or contrastive statements, 이/가 for something specific you are experiencing now

entries.label: 누구/누가 (who)
entries.usage: Place the 'who' pronoun in the subject, object or pre-이다 slot

entries.label: 뭐/무엇 (what)
entries.usage: Choose the right 'what' pronoun and decide whether a particle is used

entries.label: 몇 + counter
entries.usage: Build 'how many ___?' questions with the right counter.

entries.label: ~는/은 vs ~이/가
entries.usage: Pick the topic or subject particle and the right allomorph.
entries.example: 누가 밥을 먹었어? 내가 밥을 먹었어.

entries.label: 시간 + 후에
entries.usage: Amount of time + 후에 = '___ later / ___ from now'.
entries.example: 저는 세 시간 후에 다시 올게요.

entries.label: 의문사 + ~나 (every-)
entries.usage: 어디나 / 언제나 / 누구나 = everywhere / every time / everyone; no particles.

entries.label: 의문사 + ~ㄴ가 (some-)
entries.usage: 뭔가 / 어딘가 / 언젠가 / 누군가 = something / somewhere / sometime / somebody.

entries.label: 아무 + 나/도
entries.usage: Build 'any-' words with ~나 and 'no-' words with ~도 plus a negative verb.
